Newborn house mice weigh a single gram at birth (1 gram) [Wwb = 1 gram], a remarkably small mass that places them firmly among the most altricial of rodent neonates. This minimal initial body size necessitates an extended period of intense maternal investment, during which the altricial pups are entirely dependent on warmth and milk. The gestation period that produces these tiny offspring lasts for 20 days [tg = 20 days] when the mother is maintained at a core body temperature of 36.9 °C [T = 36.9 °C], a value consistent with the typical eutherian mammalian thermoregulatory set point. This relatively short gestation, coupled with the extremely low birth mass, allows for a rapid reproductive turnover that is a hallmark of this opportunistic murid species. The energetic cost of producing a single-gram neonate is comparatively low, enabling females to channel resources into large litters, a life-history strategy that has proven extraordinarily successful across a vast array of ecological contexts, from commensal populations in human dwellings to feral populations on remote islands.

Following the brief gestation period, female mice typically produce litters of substantial size. Under optimal laboratory conditions at 36.9 °C [T = 36.9 °C], where thermal stress is eliminated, the maximum reproductive output is considerable: females can produce approximately 5 pups per litter [N_R_i = approximately 5 pups per litter] and achieve up to seven litters each year [F_R_i = up to seven litters each year]. This prodigious fecundity translates into a population growth potential that underpins the species’ reputation as a prolific breeder. The lactating female must sustain this high output while simultaneously meeting her own metabolic needs, a physiological challenge that becomes particularly acute during the pre-weaning period. The nursing offspring, as suckling juveniles, grow rapidly, relying entirely on the mother's milk. This period of intense lactation represents the most energetically demanding phase of the female's reproductive cycle, and its successful completion is critical for pup survival and the eventual attainment of the juvenile stage.

The transition from complete dependence to nutritional independence occurs through the process of weaning. In the house mouse, this milestone is reached at 22 days after birth [tx = 22 days after birth] under standard thermal conditions at 36.9 °C [T = 36.9 °C]. At this point, the pups shift from a diet of maternal milk to solid food, marking the cessation of lactation and the onset of dietary independence. Weaning is not an abrupt event but a gradual process, during which the mother reduces nursing frequency and the pups increasingly explore and consume solid food items. The timing of this transition is critical: weaning too early can lead to malnutrition and increased vulnerability, while delayed weaning may reduce the mother's capacity to initiate a subsequent pregnancy. By 22 days after birth [tx = 22 days after birth], the young are typically fully independent and begin to disperse, a behavior that facilitates the colonization of new territories and contributes to the species’ remarkable invasive success across diverse habitats at a temperature of 36.9 °C [T = 36.9 °C].

Sexual development in the female house mouse follows a precise temporal schedule, culminating in the attainment of puberty. The vagina, which remains closed at birth, undergoes a clear morphological change that signals the onset of reproductive competence. Specifically, the vagina opens at approximately 26 days after birth [tp = approximately 26 days after birth], a developmental landmark documented at a standard body temperature of 36.9 °C [T = 36.9 °C]. At this stage, the animal's body mass has increased dramatically from its one-gram birth weight to a wet weight at puberty of about 10 grams [Wwp = about 10 grams]. This tenfold increase in mass reflects the substantial growth that occurs during the suckling and immediate post-weaning juvenile period. The timing of vaginal opening is a reliable external indicator that the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis has become active, and it typically precedes the first estrous cycle by a short interval. This rapid sexual maturation allows young females to contribute to the breeding population soon after they have achieved nutritional independence.

Adult house mice reach a moderate body size that reflects their opportunistic, high-fecundity life-history strategy. An adult individual can attain an ultimate wet weight of 50 grams [Wwi = 50 grams] and a total body length of 10.2 centimeters [Li = 10.2 centimeters], dimensions that place them among the smaller members of the family Muridae. This relatively small adult body size is offset by an extraordinarily rapid life cycle and high reproductive output. In terms of body composition, the whole-body energy density measured in dry weight, excluding any reproductive tissues, averages approximately 20.1 kilojoules per gram  when assessed at the species' thermoneutral body temperature of 36.9 °C [T = 36.9 °C]. This energy density, calculated from a mean value spanning neonates to adults, reflects the calorific content of somatic tissues and provides a useful baseline for constructing bioenergetic models of growth and metabolism. The combination of a high energy density, rapid maturation, and substantial reproductive output has made Mus musculus an exceptionally successful colonizer, capable of establishing sustainable populations across a remarkable diversity of ecological conditions.
